meta.title: Who really said "The path to paradise begins in hell"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Widely pinned on Dante, but this exact line is in no canto or translation of the Divine Comedy — it's a modern paraphrase of the poem's Hell-to-Paradise arc.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The path to paradise begins in hell'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Dante everywhere online, yet absent from the Divine Comedy and Wikiquote. A modern one-line condensation of the poem's arc, not his words.

answer.label: Not Dante Alighieri — a modern paraphrase
answer.authorDates: c. 1265 – 1321 · Florentine poet, author of the Divine Comedy
answer.sourceLine: The neat English aphorism is not found in any canto or standard translation of Dante’s work; it is a modern condensation of the poem’s structure — the pilgrim reaches Paradiso only after passing through Inferno. The underlying idea is genuinely Dante’s; this exact wording is not.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Modern paraphrase — not in Dante’s text

source.excerpt: The path to paradise begins in hell.
trail: The line is served up by quote aggregators crediting Dante — e.g. Goodreads ↗ — but with no cited canto, translation, or edition, and the site itself notes such quotes are “not verified.”
It is absent from both the sourced and the Misattributed sections of Dante’s Wikiquote page ↗, which does document his genuine lines such as “Abandon all hope, you who enter here.”
It appears in no standard English translation of the Divine Comedy ↗; it condenses the poem’s three-realm arc into one aphorism.
source.excerptNote: No primary source exists for this sentence. It compresses the journey of the Divine Comedy — descent through Hell (Inferno), ascent of the mountain of purgation (Purgatorio), and arrival in Heaven (Paradiso) — into a single modern line Dante never wrote.
source.rightsNote: Because the exact wording matches no located primary source and is an anonymous modern paraphrase with no identifiable first publication, no copyright status can be responsibly asserted. Dante’s medieval Italian original is long in the public domain, but that is a different text from this English line.

author.name: Dante Alighieri
author.heading: About Dante Alighieri
author.metaLine: c. 1265–1321 · Florentine poet, author of the Divine Comedy
author.bio: Dante Alighieri was a Florentine poet whose Divine Comedy (c. 1308–1321) traces an allegorical journey from the depths of Hell through Purgatory to the vision of God in Paradise. Its architecture — salvation reached only by first confronting sin and suffering — is exactly the thought this modern one-liner tries to capture, even though the sentence itself is not his.

cite.sourceCitation: No primary source located. Earliest documented usage is in undated online quotation aggregators (e.g. Goodreads, AZQuotes) crediting Dante Alighieri without citing any canto, translation, or edition of the Divine Comedy.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: A textbook “magnet-name” quote: a tidy modern maxim pinned on a famous author because it sounds like something he’d say — and, structurally, it is. But sounding right is not the same as being written.

items.why: No canto or standard translation of the Divine Comedy contains this sentence, and it does not appear among Dante’s sourced quotations on Wikiquote ↗. Quote sites such as Goodreads ↗ attach his name with no work, canto, or translation cited.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea — that Paradise is reached only by first passing through Hell — genuinely maps onto Dante’s poem, whose pilgrim descends through Inferno before ascending to Paradiso. The compact English aphorism, however, is a later condensation, not a line Dante wrote. See his actual verse on Wikiquote ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Dante’s Divine Comedy is built as a single upward journey: the pilgrim can only reach the light of Paradise by first descending through the whole of Hell and then climbing the terraces of Purgatory. That structure is so memorable that it invites exactly this kind of summary — a one-sentence moral of the whole poem.

The problem is that the summary has been promoted from paraphrase to quotation. Stripped of quotation marks around whose words they are, aggregator sites present the modern gloss as if Dante penned it, and it circulates as a verified line when no primary text supports it.
context.pull: The thought is Dante’s architecture; the sentence is a modern caption for it.
